architecture.diagramAria: Your app, Stripe, GitHub and Shopify send webhooks to the Railhook API, which checks the providers' signatures and stores each event in PostgreSQL before replying, then passes it through Kafka to the worker. The worker delivers to your customers and your services and retries what fails; both use PostgreSQL, and Redis for rate limits and ordering.

signing.body: Endpoint and source signing secrets and mTLS client keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Encryption keys are versioned, and an operator can re-encrypt every secret under a new one.

apiKeys.body: A project API key is shown once, when it is created. Railhook keeps only its SHA-256 hash. A key can be rotated with a grace period, or revoked.

sessions.body: Access tokens last 15 minutes. The refresh token sits in an HttpOnly cookie and is replaced on every use; if a used one is presented again, every session of that user ends. You can see your sessions and end any of them.

tenancy.title: Organizations are isolated
tenancy.body: Every database query is scoped to the caller's organization by the data layer itself, lookups by id included, so no feature depends on remembering the check. Another organization's resource answers 404.

abuse.title: Limits on abuse

signed.title: Every delivery is signed
signed.body: HMAC-SHA256 over the payload, in Railhook's own header and in the Standard Webhooks format. After a secret is rotated, deliveries are signed with both secrets for 24 hours, so receivers switch without downtime.

incoming.title: Incoming webhooks are verified
incoming.body: Stripe, GitHub, GitLab, Shopify, Slack and Twilio requests are checked with each provider's own scheme before anything is stored. A request that fails is answered 401 and not stored, and a replayed signature is refused.

network.title: No requests into private networks
network.body: Endpoint URLs are checked when they are saved and again before every attempt. Loopback, link-local and private addresses are refused, so a webhook cannot be aimed at internal services.

mtls.title: Client certificates and ownership checks

how.title: How each provider signs
how.lead: What is signed, with which key, and where the signature goes. Every scheme here is HMAC-SHA256.
how.standard: Signs webhook-id.webhook-timestamp.body with the base64-decoded whsec_ secret. The webhook-signature header carries v1,<base64>, one entry per active secret. The timestamp is in seconds, with a 5-minute window.
how.stripe: Signs t.body with the whsec_ secret as written. Stripe-Signature carries t=<seconds>,v1=<hex>, one v1 per active secret, with a 5-minute window.
how.github: Signs the raw body. X-Hub-Signature-256 carries sha256=<hex>. There is no timestamp.
how.shopify: Signs the raw body. X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256 carries the digest in base64. There is no timestamp.
how.slack: Signs v0:timestamp:body. X-Slack-Signature carries v0=<hex>, and X-Slack-Request-Timestamp the time in seconds, with a 5-minute window.
how.railhook: Signs t.body with the endpoint secret. X-Signature carries t=<milliseconds>,v1=<hex>, with a 5-minute window. Railhook sends the Standard Webhooks headers as well.

cta.title: Stop losing webhooks

pollingVsPush.aria: Two rows on one timeline. Polling: your code sends GET /orders on a timer, six times; the first four replies are "nothing new", the order is created just after the fourth, and only the fifth request finds it, up to one polling interval late — six requests, one useful. Webhook: at the instant the order is created, the sender makes one POST to your endpoint — one request, one useful.
pollingVsPush.caption: Polling pays for every empty answer and still hears about the order up to one interval late. A webhook costs one request and arrives when the event happens.

polling.title: Polling
polling.lag: up to one polling interval late

webhookAnatomy.aria: An annotated webhook request. The request line says where it goes: a URL the receiver registered. The webhook-id header is its identity, the same on every retry and the key to deduplicate on. The webhook-timestamp header is its freshness: reject it when it is older than about five minutes. The webhook-signature header is the proof: an HMAC-SHA256 of the id, the timestamp and the body. The JSON body says what happened: the event type and its data.
webhookAnatomy.caption: Three headers carry everything a receiver needs to trust the request: which event it is, when it was sent, and proof that nobody changed it on the way.

target.title: Where
target.body: a URL the receiver registered for this event

id.title: Identity
id.body: the same on every retry: your deduplication key

timestamp.title: Freshness
timestamp.body: older than ~5 minutes? reject: the replay window

body.title: What happened
body.body: the event type, and its data

receiverAck.aria: Three lanes against the sender's timeout. The handler verifies the signature, records the event id and enqueues the event, then answers 200 OK well inside the timeout. A worker picks the event up from the queue and does the slow work — email, stock, other APIs — with nobody waiting. Doing the same work inside the handler runs past the timeout, so the sender counts a failure and retries.
receiverAck.caption: Acknowledge inside the budget, work outside it. The handler's only job is to make the event safe; the worker's job is everything else.
receiverAck.work: award points · email a receipt · call the warehouse
receiverAck.inlineWork: the same work, in the request
receiverAck.workNote: as long as it takes; a failure is yours to retry

retryBackoff.aria: Two timelines on a logarithmic axis from now to one day, with the endpoint down for the first three hours. With retries on the Standard Webhooks example schedule, attempts at 0, 5 seconds, about 5 minutes, 35 minutes and 2 hours 35 minutes fail during the outage, and the attempt at 7 hours 35 minutes is delivered. With a single attempt, the event fails at once and is lost unless someone redelivers it.
retryBackoff.caption: The Standard Webhooks example schedule against a three-hour outage, as time since the first attempt on a log scale. Back-off turns an outage into a delay; a single attempt turns it into a loss.

once.title: One attempt
once.result: failed: lost unless someone redelivers it

duplicateDelivery.aria: A sequence between a sender and a receiver. The first POST, with webhook-id msg_2mQ8…, is processed and the order recorded, but the 200 response is lost to a timeout. The sender retries with the same webhook-id. The receiver has already stored that id, skips the work and answers 200 OK. Without the check, the retry would create a second order.
duplicateDelivery.caption: A retry after a lost response is the most ordinary duplicate there is. The id that stays the same across retries is what makes the second arrival harmless.
duplicateDelivery.without: without the check: a second order

outOfOrder.aria: Three events in the order they happened — order.created, order.updated, order.cancelled — and the order they arrived in: updated, cancelled, and created last, because its first attempt failed and it came back as a retry. Updated and cancelled are applied; created is skipped, because its version is older than the one already stored.
outOfOrder.caption: Arrival order is whatever the network and the retries made it. A version check turns a late order.created from a resurrection into a no-op.
outOfOrder.rule: apply an event only if its version is newer than what you have

secretRotation.aria: Two timelines of a secret rotation. With an overlap, the old secret keeps signing after the rotation until it is retired, so between the rotation and your deploy each request carries two v1 signatures and one of them always verifies. Without an overlap, the old secret stops the instant it is rotated, and every request between the rotation and your deploy fails verification.
secretRotation.caption: Rotation without an overlap is an outage you scheduled yourself. Signing with both secrets for a while — Stripe allows up to 24 hours — lets the receiver deploy whenever it is ready.

overlap.title: With an overlap
overlap.result: two v1 signatures per request: either one verifies

providerRetries.aria: A timeline comparing how long three providers keep trying an endpoint that is down. Stripe backs off exponentially for up to three days. GitHub makes one attempt with a ten-second timeout and never retries on its own, leaving a three-day window in which you can redeliver by hand. Shopify makes up to eight calls inside four hours, and removes the webhook subscription after repeated failure within a day.
providerRetries.caption: Three policies on one axis, log-scaled so the first minute is as visible as the third day. Every figure is sourced in the table below.

retryLadder.aria: A bar chart of the wait before each Railhook retry of an outgoing delivery: one minute, five minutes, fifteen minutes, one hour, six hours and twenty-four hours, drawn on a log scale.
retryLadder.caption: Railhook's default ladder for outgoing deliveries: seven attempts, the last of them a day after the first. Incoming relays use a shorter one on purpose.

gateway.aria: A pipeline: a provider sends once, on its own schedule, to a gateway that verifies the signature, drops duplicates and stores the event; the gateway then delivers to your app on its own retry ladder, and any stored event can be replayed for seven days.
gateway.caption: The provider's schedule stops mattering at the first box. What reaches your app is on a ladder you own, from a copy you can replay.

app.title: Your app
app.body: gets it when it is up

dualWrite.aria: Three timelines of the same event, each with a process crash in it. Commit, then publish: the event is committed and the client told 201, the process dies, the publish never runs, and the event is accepted but never delivered. Publish, then commit: the message reaches Kafka, the commit fails and rolls back, the client gets an error and retries, and a worker receives a message about a row that does not exist. Outbox: the event and its outbox row are committed together, the client told 201, the process dies, and on restart the publisher finds the pending row and publishes it, so the event is delivered late and perhaps twice, but never lost.
dualWrite.caption: The same crash in three places. Only the ordering that never has to do two things at once survives it, and its cost is that a message can go out twice.

outboxPipeline.aria: The pipeline. The API receives POST /api/v1/events and, in one Postgres transaction, writes the event, one delivery per matching subscription and one outbox row per delivery, then answers 201. A publisher polls the outbox every second with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and produces each row to Kafka's deliveries.dispatch topic, keyed by endpoint id. A worker consumes the message, claims the delivery row in Postgres with a fence token, and the Attempt Runner sends the signed request to the endpoint, whose webhook-id header is the delivery id. A failure goes back to Postgres as next_retry_at for the retry ladder.
outboxPipeline.caption: Kafka carries the news; Postgres keeps the obligation. Every arrow after the first box can fail and be tried again, because the rows it announces are already committed.

orderingHold.aria: A timeline of four ordered deliveries to one endpoint. Sequence 1 fails its first attempt at zero seconds and waits on its retry ladder; its second attempt succeeds at about 44 seconds. Sequences 2, 3 and 4 arrive a few seconds apart and are parked, which is a deferral and spends no attempt. When sequence 1 succeeds, they are released and delivered in order. A dashed line at 63 seconds marks the gap timeout, sixty seconds after sequence 2 was first parked: had sequence 1 still been failing by then, the parked deliveries would have gone without it.
orderingHold.caption: Ordering is a hold, not a wall. A predecessor that recovers inside the gap timeout keeps the order; one that does not is overtaken, and webhook_ordering_gap_timeout_total counts it. The timings are illustrative; the 60-second default is not.
orderingHold.parked: parked: a Deferral, no Attempt spent

deliverySemantics.aria: A table of delivery semantics against two failures. In the first, the request is lost on the way and the receiver never sees it. In the second, the receiver processes the request and the response is lost. The sender sees the same thing in both: a timeout. At-most-once never resends, so the first case loses the event and the second processes it once. At-least-once resends until it hears back, so the first case processes it once and the second processes it twice. Exactly-once would need the sender to tell the two cases apart, which it cannot. At-least-once with the receiver deduplicating on webhook-id processes the event once in both cases.
deliverySemantics.caption: The sender cannot tell a lost request from a lost response. Exactly-once delivery would need it to; exactly-once effect only needs the receiver to remember what it has done.
deliverySemantics.sees: what the sender sees in both: a timeout

exactlyOnce.name: exactly-once
exactlyOnce.cell: needs to know which column it is in

aiHarnessLoop.aria: A loop of eight steps. Top row, left to right: a task file the person writes, the rules and skill the agent loads, a failing test, the implementation. Bottom row, right to left: local checks, CI, release and a deploy a named person approves, and a verification from outside. Local checks and CI can refuse a change and send it back to the agent. Anything that still gets through becomes an incident, and each incident becomes a new rule, skill or ratchet that feeds back into the rules the agent loads.
aiHarnessLoop.caption: The engineering loop around the agent. The agent owns three steps of eight; the person owns the task and the deploy; machine checks own the rest. The arrow along the right-hand side is the one that makes it improve.
aiHarnessLoop.incident: Incident → new rule, skill or ratchet

aiBugGuardrail.aria: Six bugs and the guardrail each became. Large events sent as a compressed blob, found in a review, now refused by a check that both services agree with the database. An incoming pipeline copied from the outgoing one, found in a review, now one shared implementation. A raw SQL insert failing every night, found during tenancy work, now a check on every raw query. Squash merges into main, noticed at the next release merge, now blocked by a branch setting. A worker started before migrations, seen in the restart count, now an upgrade-order test. A field that zoomed on an iPhone, seen in production, now a browser test at phone and desktop widths.
aiBugGuardrail.caption: Bug, how it was noticed, and what now refuses it. Each guardrail has the shape of the bug that created it.

lostAck.aria: A timeline with two lanes, the Railhook worker above and your endpoint below. The worker sends attempt 1 carrying webhook-id d-42. Your endpoint does the work and commits it: the order is marked paid. Its 200 response is lost on the way back. All the worker sees is silence until its 30-second timeout, and at that moment it cannot tell whether the request was lost, is still being processed, or was processed and answered. It sends attempt 2 with the same webhook-id, and the endpoint's dedupe recognises it and answers 2xx without doing the work again.
lostAck.caption: The only duplicate Railhook cannot stop. The receiver has committed; the sender has seen nothing. Resending is the only way not to lose the event, and the unchanged webhook-id is the only way the receiver can tell.
lostAck.question: lost? slow? done?
